opus-5.5.text:
I think the Google internship was a really important turning point for me, though maybe not in the way people would expect. When you're a PhD student, you tend to think about research as a very individual thing. You have your advisor, your own small problem, and you try to squeeze out a paper. Going into an industry lab like that, I suddenly saw a completely different scale of thinking: the compute, the infrastructure, and especially the people. You'd have lunch with someone, and they would casually talk about an idea that later became a whole research direction.

What it taught me, more than any specific technical skill, was taste. What problems are worth working on? What's a "real" problem versus something that just looks good on a benchmark table? In academia, especially early on, you're often optimizing for getting the paper accepted. At Google I saw people who were much more willing to take a long view, to build something general and simple instead of something clever and narrow. That idea that simplicity and generality are worth more than incremental tricks has stayed with me. A lot of what I care about now, things like scalable architectures, representation learning, and trying to find principles instead of hacks, partly traces back to that experience.

It also gave me some confidence. Before that, I wasn't sure whether my way of thinking would hold up in that environment. Working alongside very strong researchers and seeing that my ideas could contribute was meaningful for a young student.

That said, I don't want to romanticize it. An internship is short, maybe three months. You don't fully own anything, and you're working within someone else's agenda. So I see it as one piece of a larger path: the PhD training gave me depth, the internships gave me exposure and perspective, and later, moving between industry and academia, I could combine the two. If I had to summarize it, the internship didn't define my research, but it widened my sense of what research could be.

r001.rationale: The response describes the internship as broadening Xie’s perspective, but does not attribute dissertation fragmentation to internships on topics he had not previously worked on.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the Google internship was a turning point, though not quite in the way I expected going in.

I went there, I think it was 2015 or so, during my PhD at UC San Diego with Zhuowen Tu. Before that, my work was more rooted in the traditional computer vision way of thinking. You care about the problem, you design features, you reason very carefully about structure. At Google, I was suddenly surrounded by people who thought at a completely different scale. Infrastructure was abundant, and more importantly, people were comfortable letting the data and the compute do a lot of the work that we used to do by hand.

What that did for me was shift my intuition about where the leverage is. I started to see that architecture and the training recipe matter enormously, and that simple, scalable designs tend to win over clever but fragile ones. That mindset fed directly into ResNeXt, which came a bit later at Facebook with Kaiming He and others. The idea of "aggregated transformations" with a very regular, repeatable structure is really a bet on simplicity and scalability, and I don't think I would have made that bet with the same conviction without having seen how industry teams actually operated.

The other thing I'd say is that internships taught me how to collaborate with people who are much better than me at certain things. In academia you can get a bit isolated and start believing you need to do everything yourself. At Google I learned how to be one piece of a much larger effort, and to be comfortable with that. That's a skill I still rely on now, running a lab at NYU and working with industry partners.

So I'd assess it as less about any specific paper that came out of it, and more about recalibrating my taste. It changed what I thought a "good" research question looked like, and it made me less afraid of ideas that seemed too simple to be interesting.

r001.rationale: The response describes the Google internship as changing Xie’s research intuition and collaboration style, but does not attribute dissertation fragmentation to internships or say they involved topics he had not previously worked on.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as one step in developing my taste as a researcher. An internship gives you a chance to step outside your usual environment and see how other people approach problems—what questions they ask, what evidence they find convincing, and when they decide an idea is worth pursuing.

In the context of my broader development, that’s the lens I would use to assess the Google experience: not just what came out of that period, but how it helped me think more independently about what I wanted to work on next.
